en: Mother, I have lost you.
Having lost you, mother,
Alas, I yearn for a single sight of you.
Over cliffs no dog would cross,
Kanykei, you went on foot.
Is this the time for Bakai to howl?
On cliffs no dog would cross,
With my steel blunted,
How can I remain alive,
Alas, having lost my orphan?
My wing broken,
Is this the time for Bakai to lament?
Parted from my orphan,
My burning lamp,
O, parted from one who cared for me,
Am I to stand here burning in grief?
O, if I cannot see him, there is no life.
Shall I sever this buried life?
Parted from my orphan,
Am I to remain alive and not die?
O my precious Manas, remain alive;
Bakai, may you never see such torment!
Such nights of calamity
May you never grant your servant!
O my beloved friend Manas, remain alive;
May this wretched life never know sorrow!
Parted from my support,
Such humiliation
May you never grant your servant!
Parted from Kozhosan,
That I would become wretched—
Why did I not see it from the start?
O alas, with my friend Manas,
Instead of remaining alive, I, Bakai—
Why did I not die?
When my precious world was beside me,
When Khan Manas was alive,
Kara-Shaar and Kambyl—
When I was besieging them,
Their kaldais and lungtungs—
When I was beating them,
When the broad world grew narrow,
When Khan Manas was alive,
Why did I not die then?
To the unbelievers, whatever I wished—
When I was doing that,
Slitting the Chinese throats like sheep,
When I was slaughtering them,
To the world, whatever I wished—
When I was doing that,
Breaking Ombu and taking booty,
Breaking through its midst and opening a road,
Loading elephants and taking gold coins,
When I swelled with pride,
When Khan Manas was alive,
O, why did I not die then!
How shall I see my only one?
Let me die now, not remain alive.
O this beard no enemy dared touch,
Now you are shorn as though an enemy struck.
This mustache on which ice never froze,
Now you are cruelly torn out without leave.
O Almighty, whose command is strong,
Why have you decreed so much?
Parted from my orphan,
I have perished in a place of hardship.
Having lost Kanykei,
My poor self has come to ruin.
Your uncle Bakai, the gray-maned hero,
His beard left bristling,
O, the widow left in the cave was gone;
His mustache stood ragged.
Without looking up or down,
Mighty Bakai stood ready to die,
Not sparing his life from death.
“When I went to Talas,
My widow and my orphan—
Did someone lying in wait attack them?
Chyiyrdy, grown old—
Did they splash her blood like a bulat blade?
My only cradle-infant—
Did they wrench him from her hands?
Did God the smiter strike them?
Did he make it like an extinguished fire?
Old King Bakai's
Back—has it been broken so?
Thinking to seek ample provisions,
Parted from my blessing,
Has God struck me down?”
Then your uncle Bakai,
Urging on the gray winged steed,
Stood at the mouth of the cave.
“Kanykei!” he called aloud,
Roaring in anger,
As though the disgraced woman were watching,
Unable to endure his grief,
Calling out “Kanykei!”
Then your uncle Bakai said:
“Kanykei, born only for sorrow—
Has she scattered her travel provisions?
Unable to endure staying in the cave,
Unable to remain, panting and burning with grief,
Did she lose all recourse and hurry away?
Toward her father's city of Bukhara,
Grieving and weeping without cease,
Taking up the orphan,
Did she set out as her heart desired?
This noble child of mine, Kanykei,
Was an ill-willed soul.
She never retreated at the word of death,
Never drew back from dying;
Her fortunes were complete.
Indeed, my child Kanykei
Was a lion among women.
To my tiger, gray-maned Manas,
She was the Night of Power he encountered.
Revered Kanykei
Was a handmaid like a saint.
This Aman-Jol here
To her father's city of Bukhara,
Coming and going, Kanykei
Had traveled and knew this road.
Unable to stay grieving and weeping,
Did she scatter the wild sheep's meat?
Taking her mother on her back,
Did she flee toward Temir Khan?”
Saying this, mighty Bakai
Through the swaying green grass
Went searching to and fro, mighty Bakai.
Sorrow-stricken Kanykei's
Tracks he found upon the road;
The hero Bakai moved from side to side.
On the gentle, open slope,
He saw the prints of her steps.
The rounded, brushy ridge—
He saw where she had crossed it.
The great poplar where she had halted,
The great and sacred shrine—
He saw where she had lain.
The winding stream—
He saw where she had forded it.
The single road running alongside
Was the road to Bukhara.
With tails trailing behind them,
Foxes would not travel that road.
With ears standing erect,
Wolves would not travel that road.
There was no hill as big as an ankle-bone,
No hollow as big as a saddlecloth,
No furrow touched by a plow,
No burrow dug by a marmot.
Across the moon-like yellow plain,
Your old uncle Bakai
Traveled along,
Closely following her trail.
Longing for the orphan,
He pursued them until he grew sallow.
Following their tracks closely in the sand,
Your wretched uncle Bakai
Pursued them until he grew pale.
Among the glossy dark thorns,
Kanykei, weeping helplessly,
Stood in that place.
Her joints gave way as she sobbed;
Chyiyrdy rode upon her,
Semetey was in her arms;
Bereft of any recourse, she cried out.
Her soles were pounded by stones,
Her temples scorched by the sun.
She found no cold water for her thirst,
No poison to end her life,
Nor, to take shelter in the shade,
A cooler place;
To die without further exhaustion,
She found no ready grave.
Dust covered and filled her mouth.
From a spring crossing her path, from running water,
Kanykei yearned for a single swallow.
Parted from her falcon,
Your bereft widow could not stand,
Reduced to such wretchedness.
Her gray-maned uncle Bakai—
She yearned for even one sight of him.
All her ribs and bones
Seemed to crack, collapse and come apart.
The dark blood flowing from her calves
Poured down into her boots.
The lady screamed in misery;
To reach her father Temir Khan
Your sister-in-law yearned terribly.
She had grown utterly exhausted.
When your mother cried “Oh!” blood came from her mouth.
Thirsty and hungry alike,
Your mother Kanykei lost her strength.
In mortal anguish she took as her support
Her one child Semetey;
Hungry, truly suffering hell,
Her thoughts scattered far and wide.
Clasping him with all her life,
Kanykei took as her support
The child left by the valiant warrior.
“Such is this wretched world,” she thought.
The noble woman Kanykei
Troubled her heart still more.
Following the trail, Bakai saw
The child she was carrying.
The horse Bakai led was Taitoru;
On Bakai's right was Akborchuk.
With a letter written for Bukhara,
Weeping and sobbing, for his orphan,
With two swift horses,
He had come searching.
Your father Bakai brought good fortune;
His lofty support was like a countless army.
When he saw Kanykei's figure,
He groaned with grief:
“Alas, leopard Manas, do not die!
Alas for this world!
When the khan dies, all have died;
Women and children crying out,
May you never wander in this way!
If it has happened so to her,
To whom might it not happen?
Such humiliation,
From now on, one God,
Do not grant your servant!” he said.
“God, do not take the lion!
Such humiliation
Do not impose upon your servant again!
Descendants of noble lords,
May you never be left wandering in the wilderness like this!
God, do not take the khan!
The only child of the prince,
Fleeing in fear to Bukhara,
May you never wander stripped of your dignity!
May no widow be left behind!
Bakai in his old age—
Do not lift him up and plunge him into misery!
Setting out toward Temir Khan,
Were you, fierce woman, meant to wander?
Roaming in search, unable to find you,
Was I, Bakai, meant to stare helplessly?
Walking on foot without boots,
Were you, my child, meant to sob?
Neither dying nor vanishing in the wilderness,
Was I, Bakai, meant to roar in grief?
When your royal lord died,
My child, fierce Kanykei,
Were you meant to flee in your stockings?
Parted from my orphan,
Still going about without sinking into the earth,
Was I, peerless Bakai, meant for this?
When my king Manas was alive,
Did I eat a raven's eye?
Unable to find his only child,
Alas, King Bakai—
